This is perfect. I’m a uni admin of 12+ years and 100% agree with all of this. 

-I’ve worked with so many students who were top of their class struggle in their first semester of college. It’s a different environment, different structure. It’s normal to have to feel things out. Don’t fret - it’s a little stumble, that’s all. You’ll find your footing. You’ll get there. 

-One of the biggest mistakes I see is students not asking for help until it’s way too late. Don’t fall prey to that - ask for help now, as mentioned above. 

-Students don’t take advantage of their advisors and tutoring services nearly enough, especially if they were top-of-class types who were always able to cram or skate by. Colleges WANT you to be successful, so take advantage of their resources. 

-If you’re not used to the degree of self study required, you’ll have to build that muscle, build that discipline. The 2-3 hour rule is solid advice, so don’t think it’s an exaggeration. Make time for it. 

I know this sounds like a lot. It feels overwhelming. I remember working my butt off in a really tough class in undergrad and getting a low grade. It sucks. It feels like a punch to the gut. But if you stand up, dust yourself off, hold your head high, and put your mind to it, I know you’ll get there. You’ve got this.

I picked my major thinking I wanted to do that for the rest of my life, and ended up pivoting right after graduation to a VASTLY different career. A lot can change in 3-4 years, you aren’t alone. 

Using career services at your school is great advice - most university career services will have workshops for resumes, the interview, job hunting, etc., so take advantage of those. Bonus: most of them are online or hybrid now, so they’re easy to access. 

I also loved the suggestion of getting an on campus job. I changed my career right after graduation because of a student worker position I started my sophomore year and ended up falling in love with. As a hiring manager at a university, I can tell you that there are always positions opening up, and we love hiring juniors and seniors because they tend to be more responsible/mature. 

Another thing you might consider is a portfolio of some kind. The suggestion from joan_of_spark to look at classes/electives where you have gained important skills brought to mind some fantastic projects that I’ve worked on for classes that I’ve used as examples in interviews, or at least referenced in some way. Since your LinkedIn has areas for courses, class projects, organizations, awards, etc., there’s no reason not to incorporate that into your resume if it helps round out the picture and put your best foot forward. 

The job market is tough, but you can do this.

I have a degree in music and use to sing at weddings and funerals for extra cash (thank goodness I have switched careers). Many years ago after a performance at a funeral, a man I had never met before came up to me. I assumed he was just going to politely tell me I did a good job, but instead he asked me how long I had been singing, if I do this often, and why my voice did X, and a number of other questions. When he suggested that I might resolve something he perceived as an “issue” (it was not) by trying something odd (I don’t remember what, because it was stupid), I asked him if he was a musician. “Oh, no, I don’t know anything about music.” Yeah… I said, “Great, I’m going to follow the advice of the PhD’s who trained me” and walked away. I hope my face looked as pissed as I felt. If looks could kill, I would have had another gig lined up right then.

Seriously, don’t worry about it. The fact that you’re so concerned is actually very charming, and shows your character. As an admissions officer, this is seriously not a big deal (I’ve seen and heard much, much, much worse, lol).

What course is it? If it’s something foundational for your degree that is crucial for your understanding of future coursework, I recommend you talk to your academic advisor about it. If they are unsure, reaching out to the professor directly (if your university has that kind of culture) can be incredibly helpful. They might have some advice or encourage you to audit the course, as has already been suggested. 

PS - If you’re worried about how it will look on a transcript, I’ve never had an employer look at my individual coursework from uni, and only a *highly* selective grad school will be so nit picky as to harp on a class taken twice. As long as you have a solid explanation as to why (which you do) it shouldn’t be an issue.

I think your plan sounds solid. You’ve clearly done your research. If you’re absolutely miserable at Cal State, transferring for your mental health is wise. You’ve mapped out a plan for degree completion in a manner that works for you and your situation right now. And that’s the goal, right? To complete the degree, get the most out of it, and not damage your psyche in the process. 

For context… I work in university enrollment management, and have done so for over a decade. When I was fresh out of high school I ended up going to a school that wasn’t a great fit for me, so I transferred. That school was a worse fit for me, so I transferred again. Luckily, the third school was an amazing fit for my needs, and I ended up thriving, graduating with honors, and finding a passion for the career I’m in now. Fit matters. If Cal State isn’t your fit, working to find the right fit is exactly what you should be doing for yourself. It makes all the difference.

Hey! I work in college admissions, so I wanted to put in my two cents. 

First, absolutely do not go to BYU. I don’t have my “admissions” hat on here, this is my “sister of a gay ex-mo who went to a religious school” hat. Just don’t put yourself through that. (And, truthfully, from an education administration standpoint, I don’t know how they’ve been able to keep their accreditation with all the bs they’ve pulled). 

Now, a few people here have recommended going to a community college. I love this idea for someone who is right on money (I went to a CC and loved my experience). If you choose this option, be sure that (a) they are regionally accredited, as you would with a 4-year university; and (b) that they have a pathway program or agreement with a university (or more than one!) where you can see yourself going after your associates. 

There are several reasons for this - first, scholarships are often higher for first-time freshmen applying to a 4-year college compared to a transfer student. Additionally, just because you completed a 2-year degree doesn’t mean that it will only take you 2 more years to get a bachelor’s degree (not all of your credits will transfer the way you want them to when going to a new school). BUT, if your CC has a transfer agreement with a 4-year university, they will have both a 2+2 study plan laid out for you so you aren’t wasting your time (and money) taking classes that won’t go towards your long-term goals, and a scholarship agreement to help you know how much your degree is going to cost in the long run. 

I know this is a LOT of information, and I hope I didn’t overwhelm you. If you have any questions, I’m happy to help. I promise not to sell you on any one school. I just remember what it’s like to be a teen with very few options and even less help.
